'''''Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry''''' '''(ABC)''' is a [[Peer review|peer-reviewed]] [[scientific journal]] publishing research articles in the broad field of analytical and bioanalytical chemistry.<ref>[https://www.springer.com/216 Journal's homepage]</ref> Some of the subjects covered are the development of instruments for [[mass spectrometry]], metallomics, ionics, and the analytical characterization of nano- and biomaterials. The journal was first published in 1862 under the name '''''Fresenius’ Journal of Analytical Chemistry'''''. In 2002 the journal was renamed to ''Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry''.

'''Organovanadium chemistry''' is the [[chemistry]] of [[organometallic compounds]] containing a [[carbon]] (C) to [[vanadium]] (V) [[chemical bond]].<ref>''Synthesis of Organometallic Compounds: A Practical Guide'' Sanshiro Komiya Ed. '''1997'''</ref> Organovanadium compounds find only minor use as reagents in [[organic synthesis]] but are significant for [[polymer chemistry]] as [[catalysts]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Design of Vanadium Complex Catalysts for Precise Olefin Polymerization|author=Kotohiro Nomura |author2=Shu Zhang |journal=Chem. [[Oxidation states]] for vanadium are +2, +3, +4 and +5. Low valency vanadium is usually stabilized with [[carbonyl]] ligands. Oxo derivatives are relatively common, unlike the organic complexes of neighboring elements.

The journal's founding [[editor-in-chief]] was Michael Hoskin ([[Cambridge University]])<ref name="JHA_ScienceHistoryPubLtd" /> and it is currently{{when|date=September 2024}} edited by James Evans ([[University of Puget Sound]]).{{cn|date=September 2024}}

{{Use mdy dates|date=May 2019}} {{short description|Observational astronomy performed with gamma rays}} [[File:Fermi 5 year 11000x6189.png|thumb|right|275px|Survey of the sky at energies above 1 GeV, collected by the [[Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope]] in five years of observation (2009 to 2013).]] [[File:Egret all sky gamma ray map from CGRO spacecraft.png|thumb|275px|The sky at energies above 100 MeV observed by the [[Energetic Gamma Ray Experiment Telescope]] (EGRET) of the [[Compton Gamma Ray Observatory]] (CGRO) satellite .]] [[File:Moon egret.jpg|thumb|right|The Moon as seen by the [[Energetic Gamma Ray Experiment Telescope]] (EGRET), in gamma rays of greater than 20 MeV. These are produced by [[cosmic ray]] bombardment of its surface.{{cite web |url=https://heasarc.gsfc.nasa.gov/docs/cgro/epo/news/gammoon.html |title=EGRET Detection of Gamma Rays from the Moon |publisher=Goddard Space Flight Center |date=August 1, 2005}}]] '''Gamma-ray astronomy''' is a subfield of [[astronomy]] where scientists [[astronomical observation|observe]] and study [[celestial object]]s and phenomena in [[outer space]] which emit cosmic [[electromagnetic radiation]] in the form of [[gamma ray]]s,Astronomical literature generally hyphenates "gamma-ray" when used as an adjective, but uses "gamma ray" without a hyphen for the noun. i.e. [[photon]]s with the highest [[photon energy|energies]] (above 100 [[electronvolt|keV]]) at the very shortest wavelengths.{{Cite journal |last=Funk |first=Stefan |date=2015-10-19 |title=Ground- and Space-Based Gamma-Ray Astronomy |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-nucl-102014-022036 |journal=Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science |language=en |volume=65 |issue= |pages=245–277 |doi=10.1146/annurev-nucl-102014-022036 |arxiv=1508.05190 |bibcode=2015ARNPS..65..245F |issn=0163-8998}} [[X-ray astronomy]] uses the next lower energy range, [[X-ray]] radiation, with energy below 100 keV. In most cases, gamma rays from [[solar flare]]s and [[Terrestrial gamma-ray flash|Earth's atmosphere]] fall in the MeV range, but it's now known that solar flares can also produce gamma rays in the GeV range, contrary to previous beliefs. Much of the detected gamma radiation stems from collisions between [[hydrogen]] gas and [[cosmic ray]]s within our [[galaxy]]. These gamma rays, originating from diverse mechanisms such as [[electron-positron annihilation]], the [[inverse Compton effect]] and in some cases [[gamma decay]],for example, supernova [[SN 1987A]] emitted an "afterglow" of gamma-ray photons from the decay of newly made radioactive [[cobalt-56]] ejected into space in a cloud, by the explosion.
{{cite web |url=http://science.hq.nasa.gov/kids/imagers/ems/gamma.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070430231515/http://science.hq.nasa.gov/kids/imagers/ems/gamma.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=April 30, 2007 |title=The Electromagnetic Spectrum - Gamma-rays |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=November 14, 2010}} occur in regions of extreme temperature, density, and magnetic fields, reflecting violent astrophysical processes like the decay of neutral [[pion]]s. They provide insights into extreme events like [[supernova]]e, [[hypernova]]e, and the behavior of matter in environments such as [[pulsar]]s and [[blazar]]s. A huge number of gamma ray emitting high-energy systems like [[black hole]]s, [[stellar corona]]s, [[neutron star]]s, [[white dwarf]] stars, remnants of supernova, clusters of galaxies, including the [[Crab Nebula]] and the [[Vela Pulsar]] (the most powerful source so far), have been identified, alongside an overall diffuse [[gamma ray|gamma-ray background]] along the plane of the [[Milky Way]] galaxy. Cosmic radiation with the highest energy triggers electron-photon cascades in the atmosphere, while lower-energy gamma rays are only detectable above it. [[Gamma-ray burst]]s, like [[GRB 190114C]], are transient phenomena challenging our understanding of high-energy [[astrophysics|astrophysical process]]es, ranging from microseconds to several hundred seconds. Gamma rays are difficult to detect due to their high energy and their blocking by the Earth’s atmosphere, necessitating balloon-borne detectors and artificial satellites in space. Early experiments in the 1950s and 1960s used balloons to carry instruments to access altitudes where the atmospheric absorption of gamma rays is low, followed by the launch of the first gamma-ray satellites: [[Small Astronomy Satellite 2|SAS 2]] (1972) and [[COS-B]] (1975). These were defense satellites originally designed to detect gamma rays from secret nuclear testing, but they discovered puzzling gamma-ray bursts coming from deep space. In the 1970s, satellite observatories found several gamma-ray sources, among which a very strong source called [[Geminga]] was later identified as a pulsar in proximity. The [[Compton Gamma Ray Observatory]] (launched in 1991) revealed numerous gamma-ray sources in space. Today, both ground-based observatories like the [[VERITAS]] array and space-based telescopes like the [[Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope]] (launched in 2008) contribute significantly to gamma-ray astronomy. This interdisciplinary field involves collaboration among physicists, astrophysicists, and engineers in projects like the [[High Energy Stereoscopic System]] (H.E.S.S.), which explores extreme astrophysical environments like the vicinity of [[black hole]]s in [[active galactic nuclei]]. Studying gamma rays provides valuable insights into extreme astrophysical environments, as observed by the H.E.S.S. Observatory. Ongoing research aims to expand our understanding of gamma-ray sources, such as blazars, and their implications for cosmology. As GeV gamma rays are important in the study of extra-solar, and especially [[Extragalactic astronomy|extragalactic]], astronomy, new observations may complicate some prior models and findings.{{cite news |url=https://www.sciencenews.org/article/strange-gamma-rays-sun-magnetic-fields |title=Strange gamma rays from the sun may help decipher its magnetic fields |work=Science News |first=Lisa |last=Grossman |date=August 24, 2018}}{{cite web |url=https://www.nasa.gov/feature/goddard/2017/nasas-fermi-sees-gamma-rays-from-hidden-solar-flares |title=NASA's Fermi Sees Gamma Rays from 'Hidden' Solar Flares |publisher=NASA |first=Francis |last=Reddy |date=January 30, 2017}} Future developments in gamma-ray astronomy will integrate data from [[gravitational wave]] and [[neutrino]] observatories ([[Multi-messenger astronomy]]), enriching our understanding of cosmic events like neutron star mergers. Technological advancements, including advanced [[mirror]] designs, better [[camera]] technologies, improved trigger systems, faster [[Readout integrated circuit|readout electronics]], high-performance photon detectors like [[Silicon photomultiplier]]s (SiPMs), alongside data processing algorithms like time tagging techniques and [[event reconstruction]] methods, will enhance [[spatial resolution|spatial]] and [[temporal resolution]]. [[Machine learning]] algorithms and [[big data]] analytics will facilitate the extraction of meaningful insights from vast datasets, leading to discoveries of new gamma-ray sources, identification of specific gamma-ray signatures, and improved modeling of gamma-ray emission mechanisms. Future missions may include space telescopes and lunar gamma-ray observatories (taking advantage of the [[Moon]]'s lack of atmosphere and stable environment for prolonged observations), enabling observations in previously inaccessible regions. The ground-based [[Cherenkov Telescope Array]] project, a next-generation gamma ray observatory which will incorporate many of these improvements and will be ten times more sensitive, is planned to be fully operational by 2025.{{Cite web |url=https://www.eso.org/public/belgium-fr/teles-instr/paranal-observatory/ctao/?lang |website=ESO.org |title=CTAO — the World's Most Powerful Ground-Based Gamma-Ray Observatory |access-date=23 May 2024}}

{{short description|Clothing and accessories incorporating computer and advanced electronic technologies}}[[File:Smartwatches.jpg|thumb|'''[[Samsung Galaxy Watch]]''' '''is designed specifically for sports and health functions, including a step counter and a heart rate monitor.''']]'''Wearable technology''' is devices that are worn on, near, or inside the human body. It can be incorporated into [[Fashion accessory|accessories]] or [[clothes|clothing]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ometov |first1=Aleksandr |last2=Shubina |first2=Viktoriia |last3=Klus |first3=Lucie |last4=Skibińska |first4=Justyna |last5=Saafi |first5=Salwa |last6=Pascacio |first6=Pavel |last7=Flueratoru |first7=Laura |last8=Gaibor |first8=Darwin Quezada |last9=Chukhno |first9=Nadezhda |last10=Chukhno |first10=Olga |last11=Ali |first11=Asad |last12=Channa |first12=Asma |last13=Svertoka |first13=Ekaterina |last14=Qaim |first14=Waleed Bin |last15=Casanova-Marqués |first15=Raúl |last16=Holcer |first16=Sylvia |last17=Torres-Sospedra |first17=Joaquín |last18=Casteleyn |first18=Sven |last19=Ruggeri |first19=Giuseppe |last20=Araniti |first20=Giuseppe |last21=Burget |first21=Radim |last22=Hosek |first22=Jiri |last23=Lohan |first23=Elena Simona |title=A Survey on Wearable Technology: History, State-of-the-Art and Current Challenges |journal=[[Computer Networks (journal)|Computer Networks]] |date=2021 |volume=193 |article-number=108074 |doi=10.1016/j.comnet.2021.108074 |doi-access=free|hdl=10234/193262 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> They typically include sensors, a processor, a power source, and wireless connectivity. This allows them to collect/provide data (movement, biometrics, environment), process it, and communicate without specific user attention. Sensor technology includes [[smartwatch]]es, [[fitness tracker]]s, [[Headphones|earbuds]], and [[smartglasses]]. It also includes medical technology such as [[Pacemaker|pacemakers]], [[Continuous glucose monitor|continuous glucose monitors]], [[neuroprosthetics]], [[Exoskeleton (human)|exoskeletons]]. and [[dual-use technology]] such as [[Night-vision device|night-vision devices]]. 

Sensing devices can detect, analyze, and transmit information such as personal vital signs, and/or ambient data and may provide immediate biofeedback.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Düking |first1=Peter |last2=Achtzehn |first2=Silvia |last3=Holmberg |first3=Hans-Christer |last4=Sperlich |first4=Billy |title=Integrated Framework of Load Monitoring by a Combination of Smartphone Applications, Wearables and Point-of-Care Testing Provides Feedback that Allows Individual Responsive Adjustments to Activities of Daily Living |journal=Sensors |date=19 May 2018 |volume=18 |issue=5 |page=1632 |doi=10.3390/s18051632 |doi-access=free |pmid=29783763 |pmc=5981295 |bibcode=2018Senso..18.1632D}}</ref><ref name=":7">{{cite journal |last1=Düking |first1=Peter |last2=Hotho |first2=Andreas |last3=Holmberg |first3=Hans-Christer |last4=Fuss |first4=Franz Konstantin |last5=Sperlich |first5=Billy |title=Comparison of Non-Invasive Individual Monitoring of the Training and Health of Athletes with Commercially Available Wearable Technologies |journal=Frontiers in Physiology |date=9 March 2016 |volume=7 |page=71 |doi=10.3389/fphys.2016.00071 |doi-access=free |pmid=27014077 |pmc=4783417 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=O'Donoghue |first1=John |last2=Herbert |first2=John |title=Data Management within mHealth Environments: Patient Sensors, Mobile Devices, and Databases |journal=Journal of Data and Information Quality |date=October 2012 |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=1–20 |doi=10.1145/2378016.2378021 }}</ref><ref>https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2023-081228 Factors influencing smartwatch use and comfort with health data sharing: a sequential mixed-method study protocol</ref><ref name="Cilliers 150–156">{{Cite journal |last=Cilliers |first=Liezel |date=2019-05-30 |title=Wearable devices in healthcare: Privacy and information security issues |journal=Health Information Management Journal |volume=49 |issue=2–3 |pages=150–156 |doi=10.1177/1833358319851684 |pmid=31146589 |issn=1833-3583}}</ref>  [[Virtual reality]] and [[augmented reality]] devices complement/supplant human senses. Viewing devices display remote content. Mechanical aids enhance physical ability. 

Wearable technology can encourage individuals to improve their lifestyle choices by providing feedback. Healthy behavior is encouraged by tracking activity levels and providing useful feedback to enable goal setting. This can be shared with interested stakeholders such as healthcare providers.<ref name="Cilliers 150–156"/> Wearables are popular in consumer electronics, most commonly in the form factors of [[smartwatches]], [[smart ring]]s, and [[Implant (body modification)|implants]]. Apart from commercial uses, wearable technology is being incorporated into navigation systems, advanced textiles ([[e-textiles]]), and [[healthcare]]. As wearable technology is being proposed for use in critical applications, like other technology, it is vetted for its reliability and security properties.<ref name=":1">{{cite book |doi=10.1145/3081333.3081351 |chapter=Characterizing Smartwatch Usage in the Wild |title=Proceedings of the 15th Annual International Conference on Mobile Systems, Applications, and Services |date=2017 |last1=Liu |first1=Xing |last2=Chen |first2=Tianyu |last3=Qian |first3=Feng |last4=Guo |first4=Zhixiu |last5=Lin |first5=Felix Xiaozhu |last6=Wang |first6=Xiaofeng |last7=Chen |first7=Kai |pages=385–398 |isbn=978-1-4503-4928-4 }}</ref>

Devices that gather data must protect user privacy. Some data may be useful to health care providers, but care must be taken to ensure that it is not misused.

'''Chemistry Central''' was a [[academic publishing|scientific publisher]] specializing in [[Open access (publishing)|open access]] publications in chemistry. It was established on August 22, 2006<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sciencebase.com/science-blog/chemistry-central.html|title=Next stop, Chemistry Central|last=Bradley|first=David|date=August 22, 2006|publisher=Sciencebase|accessdate=2009-07-31}}</ref> and was operated by [[BioMed Central]]. Along with BioMed Central and the now-defunct [[PhysMath Central]], Chemistry Central was part of "Open Access Central", representing [[open access publishing]] in [[life science]] and [[medicine]], [[physics]] and [[maths]], and [[chemistry]], respectively.<ref>{{cite web|title=Open Access Central|url=http://www.openaccesscentral.com/|accessdate=28 November 2016|date=2 February 2007|url-status=bot: unknown|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070202211201/http://www.openaccesscentral.com/|archivedate=2 February 2007}}</ref> When [[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] acquired the BioMed Central Group in 2008, Chemistry Central was transferred with it.<ref>{{cite web|title=BioMed Central sold to Springer {{!}} The Scientist Magazine®|url=http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/26808/title/BioMed-Central-sold-to-Springer/|website=The Scientist|accessdate=28 November 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Springer Acquires BioMed Central Group (BMC)|url=https://www.springer.com/gp/partners/society-zone-issues/springer-acquires-biomed-central-group--bmc-/4408|website=www.springer.com|access-date=2016-11-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307222017/http://www.springer.com/gp/partners/society-zone-issues/springer-acquires-biomed-central-group--bmc-/4408|archive-date=2016-03-07|url-status=dead}}</ref>

At the end of 2015 the Chemistry Central brand was retired, with the existing journals transferring to the [[SpringerOpen]] portfolio.<ref>{{cite web|title=Chemistry Central journals to transfer to SpringerOpen|url=http://www.springeropen.com/ccbrandchange|website=www.springeropen.com|publisher=SpringerOpen|accessdate=14 October 2016}}</ref> In January 2019, ''Chemistry Central Journal'' was renamed ''[[BMC Chemistry]]'' and brought within the [[BioMed_Central#BMC_Series|BMC Series]] journals.<ref>{{cite web|title=Chemistry Central Journal evolves to BMC Chemistry|date=28 November 2018 |url=https://blogs.biomedcentral.com/bmcblog/2018/11/28/chemistry-central-journal-evolves-to-bmc-chemistry/|accessdate=6 September 2019}}</ref>

[[Yale University]] ([[Master of Philosophy|MPhil]], [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]]) | subjects = Popular culture, art, poetry, sex, film, feminism, politics | movement = [[Individualist feminism]] | signature = Camille Paglia signature.svg | signature_size = 100px }} '''Camille Anna Paglia''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|p|ɑː|l|i|ə}} {{respell|PAH|lee|ə}}; born April 2, 1947) is an American academic, social critic, and [[Feminism|feminist]].{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69rgLvitaYM |title=Camille Paglia on her controversial feminism |date=2017-05-07 |last=CBC News: The National |access-date=2026-03-01 |via=YouTube}} Paglia was a professor at the [[University of the Arts (Philadelphia)|University of the Arts]] in [[Philadelphia]], Pennsylvania from 1984 until the university's closure in 2024.{{cite web|url= https://www.uarts.edu/staff-directory/cpaglia|title= Camille Paglia|website= Staff|publisher= U arts|access-date= May 7, 2019|archive-date= October 17, 2019|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20191017181332/https://www.uarts.edu/staff-directory/cpaglia|url-status= dead}} She is critical of many aspects of modern culture{{Cite news |newspaper=[[The Morning News (online magazine)|The Morning News]] |title=Birnbaum v. Camille Paglia |date=August 3, 2005 |first=Robert |last=Birnbaum |url= http://www.themorningnews.org/archives/birnbaum_v/camille_paglia.php | format = interview|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050805014643/http://www.themorningnews.org/archives/birnbaum_v/camille_paglia.php|archive-date=August 5, 2005|url-status=dead|author-link=}}{{Cite news |title = An atheist's defence of religion: The paradox of Camille Paglia, the cultural gunslinger|first = Richard|last = Handler|date = May 23, 2009 | work = CBC News|url = http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/an-atheist-s-defence-of-religion-1.835709}} and is the author of ''[[Sexual Personae|Sexual Personae: Art and Decadence from Nefertiti to Emily Dickinson]]'' (1990) and other books. She is also a critic of contemporary [[American feminism]] and of [[post-structuralism]], as well as a commentator on multiple aspects of [[Culture of the United States|American culture]] such as its [[Visual art of the United States|visual art]], [[Music of the United States|music]], and [[Film in the United States|film history]].

{{Short description|Jewish and Christian motif signifying divine intervention}}
[[File:Hand gottes.jpg|thumb|The hand as an isolated motif. [[Fresco]] from [[Sant Climent de Taüll]], [[Catalonia]], [[Spain]].]]
[[File:Moses and burning bush.jpeg|thumbnail|right|Moses and the Burning Bush wing panel, [[Dura Europos Synagogue]]]]
{{About|the Hand of God in art||Hand of God (disambiguation){{!}}Hand of God}}
The '''Hand of God''', or '''{{lang|la|Manus Dei}}''' in Latin, also known as '''{{lang|la|Dextera domini/dei}}''' (the "[[right hand of God]]"), is a motif in [[Jew]]ish and [[Christian art]], especially of the [[Late Antique]] and [[Early Medieval]] periods, when depiction of [[God in Judaism|Yahweh]] or [[God the Father]] as a full human figure was considered unacceptable. The hand, sometimes including a portion of an arm, or ending about the wrist, is used to indicate the intervention in or approval of affairs on Earth by God, and sometimes as a subject in itself. It is an artistic metaphor that is generally not intended to indicate that a hand was physically present or seen at any subject depicted. The Hand is seen appearing from above in a fairly restricted number of narrative contexts, often in a [[blessing]] gesture (in Christian examples), but sometimes performing an action. In later Christian works it tends to be replaced by a [[God the Father in Western art|fully realized figure of God the Father]], whose depiction had become acceptable in [[Western Christianity]], although not in [[Eastern Orthodox]] or Jewish art.<ref name="JVL Anthropomorphism">[http://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/jsource/judaica/ejud_0002_0002_0_01141.html "Anthropomorphism"], Jewish Virtual Library, especially the section on Jewish art near the end.</ref> Though the hand of God has traditionally been understood as a symbol for God's intervention or approval of human affairs, it is also possible that the hand of God reflects the anthropomorphic conceptions of the deity that may have persisted in late antiquity.<ref>Bar Ilan, 321–35; Roth, 191; C. W. Griffith and David Paulsen, 97–118; Jensen, 120–21; Paulsen, 105–16; Jill Joshowitz, ''The Hand of God:The Anthropomorphic God of Late Antique Judaism: Archaeological and Textual Perspectives'', (B.A. thesis, Yeshiva University, 2013).</ref>
 
The largest group of Jewish imagery from the ancient world, the 3rd century [[Dura-Europos synagogue|synagogue at Dura-Europos]], has the hand of God in five different scenes, including the ''Sacrifice of Isaac'',<ref>Hachlili, pp. 144–145</ref> and no doubt this was one of the many iconographic features taken over by Christian art from what seems to have been a vigorous tradition of Jewish narrative art. Here and elsewhere it often represents the ''[[bath Kol]]'' (literally "daughter of a voice") or voice of God,{{efn|A matter disputed by some scholars}} a use also taken over into Christian art.

The hand may also relate to older traditions in various other religions in the [[Ancient Near East]].<ref>Summarized by Hachlili, 145</ref> In the [[Amarna art|art of the Amarna period]] in Egypt under [[Akhenaten]], the rays of the [[Aten]] sun-disk end in small hands to suggest the bounty of the supreme deity. Like the [[hamsa]] [[amulet]], the hand is sometimes shown alone on buildings, although it does not seem to have existed as a portable [[amulet]]-type object in Christian use. It is found from the 4th century on in the [[Catacombs of Rome]], including paintings of ''Moses receiving the Law'' and the ''Sacrifice of Isaac''.<ref>Hachlili, 146</ref>

There are numerous references to the hand, or arm, of God in the [[Hebrew Bible]], most clearly metaphorical in the way that remains current in modern English, but some capable of a literal interpretation.<ref name="JVL Anthropomorphism" /> They are usually distinguished from references to a placement at the [[right hand of God]]. Later [[rabbinic literature]] also contains a number of references. There are three occasions in the gospels when the voice of God is heard, and the hand often represents this in visual art.<ref>"in Ravenna and in Western art from the ninth until the eleventh centuries" according to Schiller I, 149, although Western examples of the hand in depictions of these occasions extend well before and after these dates.</ref> [[Gertrud Schiller]] distinguishes three functions of the hand in Christian art: as symbol of either God's presence or the voice of God, or signifying God's acceptance of a sacrifice.<ref>Schiller, II 674 (Index headings)</ref>

'''Live painting''' is a form of visual [[performance art]]<ref name=CMJ>{{cite news|publisher=CMJ New Music Monthly|date=February 2000|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oSoEAAAAMBAJ&dq=%22live+painting%22+%22performance+art%22&pg=PA80|title=From Street to Center Stage|author=Neil Gladstone}}</ref> in which artists complete a [[visual art]] piece in a public performance, often at a bar, music concert, wedding reception, or public event, accompanied by a DJ or live music.<ref>{{cite news |publisher= San Francisco Chronicle |title=Berkeley: Painting in public -- Picassos play the pubs |author= Harriet Chiang |date=2005-07-22 |url= http://www.sfgate.com/cgi-bin/article.cgi?f=/c/a/2005/07/22/EBGQVDNDEA1.DTL#ixzz0Pq3zsBLb|archive-url= https://archive.today/20121216114835/http://www.sfgate.com/cgi-bin/article.cgi?f=/c/a/2005/07/22/EBGQVDNDEA1.DTL%23ixzz0Pq3zsBLb|url-status= dead|archive-date= December 16, 2012}}</ref> The artwork which is created live may be planned or improvisational.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.specialeventpainter.com/livepainting.htm |title=What is "Live Event Painting?" |publisher=Arlissa Vaughn |date= |accessdate=2014-09-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140912213143/http://www.specialeventpainter.com/livepainting.htm |archive-date=2014-09-12 |url-status=usurped }}</ref> This live art form is often contrasted with more studied [[fine art]] compositions from the same artists, which are generally executed in an [[artist studio]] or other private space.<ref>{{cite book |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=WXkjT69Q2XwC&dq=%22live+painting%22+%22performance+art%22&pg=PA31 |title= The Warhol economy: how fashion, art, and music drive New York City |publisher= Princeton University Press |author= Elizabeth Currid |page=224 |isbn= 978-0-691-12837-5 |year=2007}}</ref>

Artists in a number of genres have performed live painting, including [[LeRoy Neiman]] creating a painting during the [[1976 Summer Olympics]].<ref name=CMJ/>  In the 1990s and 2000s, live painting became a hallmark of [[street art]] and [[graffiti artist]]s, also live painting (Dancing Fingers) by Amangpintor.

'''Tropical geography''' refers to the study of places and people in the [[tropics]]. When it first emerged as a discipline, tropical geography was closely associated with [[imperialism]] and [[colonial expansion]] of the [[Colonial empire|European empires]] as contributing scholars tended to portray the [[tropical]] places as "primitive" and people "uncivilised" and "inferior".<ref name=":0">Arnold, David, 2000. "Illusory Riches": Representations of the Tropical World, 1840-1950. ''Singapore Journal of Tropical Geography''. 21(1), 2000, 6-18.</ref> A wide range of subjects has been discussed within the sub-field during late 18th to early 20th century including zoology, climatology, geomorphology, economics and cultural studies.<ref>Jarrett, H.R., 1977. ''Tropical geography: An introductory study of the humid tropics'', Macdonald and Evans, p.2.</ref>

The discipline is now more commonly known as [[development geography]] as [[colonization]] had been replaced by [[economic development]] as the main ideological driver of international and global interactions since the 1950s.<ref name=Gallaher>{{cite book |last1=Gallaher |first1=Carolyn |author-link1=Carolyn Gallaher |last2=Dahlman |first2=Carl T. |last3=Gilmartin |first3=Mary |last4=Mountz |first4=Alison |last5=Shirlow |first5=Peter |date=2009 |title=Key Concepts in Political Geography |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XpBJclVnVdQC&pg=PA118 |publisher=SAGE |location=London |pages=392 |isbn=978-1-4129-4672-8 |access-date=July 31, 2014}}</ref>{{rp|118}} Today, many scholars continue to use the term tropical geography to contest the determinism embedded in the term and de-exoticise the tropical countries and their inhabitants.

'''Auxesis''' (from the Greek word meaning increase; grow) refers to growth from an increase in [[cell size]] rather than an increase in the number of cells.  Auxetic growth occurs in certain tissues, such as [[muscle]], of the higher animals as well as in some organisms, especially [[eutelic]] ones, such as [[nematode]]s, [[tunicate]]s, and [[rotifer]]s.<ref>[http://www.tutorvista.com/content/biology/biology-iv/growth-regeneration-ageing/growth-types.php Types of Growth: Auxetic Growth, Tutor Vista]</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Juo|first=Pei-show|title=Concise Dictionary of Biomedicine and Molecular Biology|publisher=CRC Press|date=21 December 2001|page=130|isbn=9781420041309|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Y4DLBQAAQBAJ&q=auxesis+biology+research}}</ref> 

In [[plant physiology]], an auxetic substance will tend to increase [[cell growth]] without any [[cell division]]. [[Auxin]]s are auxetic [[plant hormone]]s.

'''Swimming''' has been recorded since prehistoric times; the earliest recording of [[Human swimming|swimming]] dates back to [[Stone Age]] [[Cave of Swimmers|paintings]] from around 7,000 years ago. In 1578 (or 1538, see [[Swimming (sport))]] , Nikolaus Wynmann, a [[German language|German]] professor of languages, wrote the first swimming book. Swimming was part of the first modern [[1896 Summer Olympics|Olympic games]] which was held in 1896 in [[Athens]]. In 1908, the world swimming association, [[International Swimming Federation|Fédération Internationale de Natation (FINA)]], was formed. In January 2023, the name was changed from FINA to [[World Aquatics]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-12-12 |title=FINA becomes World Aquatics as new brand launched |url=https://www.worldaquatics.com/news/2979029/fina-becomes-world-aquatics-as-new-brand-launched |access-date=2025-02-17 |website=World Aquatics |language=en}}</ref>

Swimming has been used in political contexts as well as in times of war as a way to defend a country from ancient times to the present. Swimming in the Victorian and Edwardian eras has also been connected to children's activities such as Boy Scouts, in which many scouts had to prove themselves  competent in the water, leading to the growth of swimming competitions for young people. In the modern era, swimming has played an important role in the lives of children by helping to break gender norms and by leading to calls for safety regulations around water. The addition of swimming to activities like summer camp has, advocates argue, increased youth self esteem and allowed many kids to express themselves and have fun. Swimming has also been impacted by equal rights movements, with the inclusion of women in the sport, and the inclusion of activities once considered men's events in women's swimming.

The history of [[X-ray astronomy]] begins in the 1920s, with interest in [[short wave|short wave communications]] for the [[U.S. Navy]].  This was soon followed by extensive study of the earth's [[ionosphere]]. By 1927, interest in the detection of [[X-ray]] and [[ultraviolet]] (UV) radiation at high altitudes inspired researchers to launch [[Robert Goddard|Goddard's rockets]] into the upper atmosphere to support theoretical studies and data gathering. The first successful rocket flight equipped with instrumentation able to detect [[ultraviolet|solar ultraviolet radiation]] occurred in 1946. X-ray solar studies began in 1949. By 1973 a solar instrument package orbited on [[Skylab]] providing significant solar data.<ref name=nrspcr>{{Cite web

In 1965 the [[Goddard Space Flight Center]] program in [[X-ray astronomy]] was initiated with a series of balloon-borne experiments. In the 1970s this was followed by high altitude [[sounding rocket]] experiments, and that was followed by orbiting (satellite) observatories.<ref name=goddard/>

The first rocket flight to successfully detect a cosmic source of [[Astronomical object|X-ray emission]] was launched in 1962 by a group at [[American Science and Engineering]] (AS&E).<ref name=imagine/>

X-ray wavelengths reveal information about the bodies (sources) that emit them.<ref name=Keller/>

'''Astronomy in Serbia'''  is developed in accordance with the country's [[economy of Serbia|economic capabilities]], or even slightly above them.<ref name="GAS">[[Olga Atanacković]]: [http://www.das.org.rs/mga/doc/Global%20Astronomy%20Survey_Serbia.pdf Global Astronomy Survey: Serbia] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120310074547/http://www.das.org.rs/mga/doc/Global%20Astronomy%20Survey_Serbia.pdf |date=March 10, 2012 }}</ref> [[Astronomical Observatory Belgrade]] (on [[Zvezdara]]), founded in 1887, is one of the oldest scientific institutions in Serbia.<ref name="GAS"/> Serbia is a member of the [[International Astronomical Union]] since 1935.<ref name="GAS"/>

Astronomical Observatory Belgrade remains the only professional observatory in Serbia.<ref name="GAS"/> The observatory has eight professional telescopes, and is currently{{when|date=May 2022}} completing a new station on the mountain [[Vidojevica]] near [[Prokuplje]].<ref name="GAS"/> There are also several smaller public and university observatories: the [[Despot Stefan Tower|Public Observatory]] in [[Belgrade]], [[Novi Sad Astronomical Observatory]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.adnos.org/Opserv.aspx |title=Novosadska astronomska opservatorija |accessdate=2009-11-19 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090715083440/http://adnos.org/Opserv.aspx |archivedate=2009-07-15 }}</ref> and [[Belerofont Observatory]] in [[Kragujevac]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://physics.kg.ac.rs/fizika/opservatorija/ |title=Belerofont opservatorija |accessdate=2010-06-02 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110824105710/http://physics.kg.ac.rs/fizika/opservatorija/ |archivedate=2011-08-24 }}</ref> There are two planetariums: in [[Belgrade Planetarium|Belgrade]] and [[Novi Sad Planetarium|Novi Sad]].

Astronomy is taught in primary and secondary schools, but only as a part of other courses.<ref name="GAS"/> Of great importance in teaching of astronomy is the [[Petnica Science Center]].<ref name="GAS"/> Five universities in Serbia offer the studies of astronomy: universities of [[University of Belgrade|Belgrade]], [[University of Novi Sad|Novi Sad]], [[University of Kragujevac|Kragujevac]], [[University of Niš|Niš]] and [[University of Priština (North Mitrovica)|Priština]].<ref name="GAS"/> From these, at the University of Belgrade have so far graduated 242 astronomers, and 6 astronomers at the Novi Sad; 4 more astronomers who have graduated abroad are working in Serbia.<ref name="GAS"/>

Several journals devoted to astronomy are published: ''[[Astronomija]]'',<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.astronomija.co.rs/ |title=Astronomski magazin |access-date=2019-10-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081216020517/http://www.astronomija.co.rs/ |archive-date=2008-12-16 |url-status=dead }}</ref> (discontinued since 2009), ''[[Vasiona]]'' and others.<ref name="GAS"/> Also, since 1936, a [[scientific journal]], ''[[Serbian Astronomical Journal]]'' is published.<ref name="GAS"/><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://saj.matf.bg.ac.rs/|title=Serbian Astronomical Journal|website=saj.matf.bg.ac.rs}}</ref>

In Serbia there are 17<ref name="GAS"/> associations of [[amateur astronomers]], the oldest<ref name="GAS"/><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://adrb.org/ |title=Astronomical Society "Rudjer Bošković" |access-date=2009-11-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110820222256/http://adrb.org/ |archive-date=2011-08-20 |url-status=dead }}</ref> of which is [[Astronomical Society Ruđer Bošković]].
